ab-test.label: A/B test
ab-test.definition: A controlled experiment that randomly splits users into a control group and one or more treatment groups, then compares an outcome metric between them.

p-value.label: p-value
p-value.definition: The probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one observed if there were truly no effect. It is not the probability that the result is a fluke.

lift.label: Lift
lift.definition: The relative improvement of the treatment over control on a metric, for example (treatment minus control) divided by control.

statistical-significance.label: Statistical significance
statistical-significance.definition: A result is called significant when its p-value falls below a threshold chosen in advance, commonly 0.05. It says the data would be unlikely if there were no effect, not that the effect is large or important.

type-i-error.label: Type I error
type-i-error.definition: A false positive: concluding there is an effect when there isn't one. The significance level sets how often you accept this.

type-ii-error.label: Type II error
type-ii-error.definition: A false negative: missing an effect that is really there. Its rate is one minus the test's power.

sample-size.label: Sample size
sample-size.definition: How many observations an experiment needs to reliably detect an effect of a chosen size. It depends on the baseline rate, the variance, and the error rates you accept.

default-rate.label: Default rate
default-rate.definition: The share of borrowers who fail to repay a loan within a defined period.

confidence-interval.label: Confidence interval
confidence-interval.definition: A range computed with a procedure that, over many repeated studies, would contain the true value a stated share of the time, for example 95%.

bootstrapping.label: Bootstrapping
bootstrapping.definition: Estimating uncertainty by repeatedly resampling your own data with replacement and recomputing a statistic each time.

simpsons-paradox.label: Simpson's paradox
simpsons-paradox.definition: A pattern where a trend that appears in several subgroups reverses or disappears when the groups are combined.

customer-segmentation.label: Customer segment
customer-segmentation.definition: A group of customers treated as similar for analysis, for example by size, region or behavior.

xgboost.label: XGBoost
xgboost.definition: A popular gradient-boosting library that builds many small decision trees in sequence, each one correcting the errors of the ones before it.

gradient-boosting.label: Gradient boosting
gradient-boosting.definition: An ensemble method that adds models one at a time, each trained to reduce the error that remains in the combined model so far.

logistic-regression.label: Logistic regression
logistic-regression.definition: A linear model for classification that outputs a probability. It is simple, fast and easy to explain.

auc.label: AUC
auc.definition: Area under the ROC curve: the chance that the model scores a random positive example above a random negative one. 0.5 is chance and 1.0 is perfect ranking.

test-set.label: Test set
test-set.definition: Data held back from training and used only to estimate how the model will perform on new data.

production-model.label: Model in production
production-model.definition: A model serving real predictions to real users or downstream systems, as opposed to being evaluated offline.

model-drift.label: Model drift
model-drift.definition: Decline in a deployed model's performance over time because the world, or the data it sees, has changed since it was trained.

model-degradation.label: Model degradation
model-degradation.definition: A measurable drop in a deployed model's quality compared with when it launched, whatever the cause.

monitoring.label: Model monitoring
monitoring.definition: Tracking a deployed model's inputs, predictions and outcomes to catch problems early.

alerting.label: Alerting
alerting.definition: Automatic notifications when a monitored value crosses a threshold, so someone can act.

cash-collection-forecast.label: Cash collection forecast
cash-collection-forecast.definition: A prediction of when, and how much of, the money owed on invoices will actually be received.

cash-flow-forecast.label: Cash flow forecast
cash-flow-forecast.definition: A prediction of the money coming in and going out over a future period.

forecast-horizon.label: Forecast horizon
forecast-horizon.definition: How far into the future a forecast looks, for example 90 days or 12 months. Accuracy generally worsens as the horizon grows.

forecasting.label: Forecasting
forecasting.definition: Predicting future values of a quantity from past data and known drivers.

time-series.label: Time series
time-series.definition: Data recorded over time in order, where the sequence matters because observations are usually related to nearby ones.

backtesting.label: Backtesting
backtesting.definition: Evaluating a forecasting method by replaying history: at each past date, use only what was known then, predict forward, and compare with what happened.

cross-validation.label: Cross-validation
cross-validation.definition: Estimating performance by training and evaluating on several different splits of the data and averaging the results.

k-fold.label: k-fold
k-fold.definition: A cross-validation scheme that splits the data into k parts and takes turns holding each one out for evaluation.

feature-engineering.label: Feature engineering
feature-engineering.definition: Turning raw data into inputs a model can learn from, such as ratios, counts over a time window or encoded categories.

feature-importance.label: Feature importance
feature-importance.definition: A score for how much each input feature contributes to a model's predictions. Different methods can rank the same features differently.

data-pipeline.label: Data pipeline
data-pipeline.definition: A sequence of automated steps that moves data from its sources, transforms it, and delivers it for use, such as model training.

data-validation.label: Data validation
data-validation.definition: Automated checks that data meets expectations (types, ranges, missing values, freshness) before it is used.

data-quality.label: Data quality
data-quality.definition: How well data fits its purpose: accurate, complete, consistent, timely and free of unwanted duplicates.

churn.label: Churn
churn.definition: When a customer stops using or paying for a product. The churn rate is the share lost in a period.

cohort.label: Cohort
cohort.definition: A group of users who share a starting point, typically the period they signed up, tracked together over time.

retention.label: Retention
retention.definition: The share of a group that is still active some time after they started.

window-function.label: Window function
window-function.definition: A SQL function that computes a value for each row using a set of related rows (its window) without collapsing them into one row.

top-n-per-group.label: Top N per group
top-n-per-group.definition: A common SQL pattern: keep only the N highest-ranked rows within each group, such as each department.

rolling-average.label: Rolling average
rolling-average.definition: An average over a sliding window of recent values, used to smooth out day-to-day noise.

sessionization.label: Sessionization
sessionization.definition: Grouping a stream of user events into sessions, usually by starting a new one after a long enough gap.

anti-join.label: Anti-join
anti-join.definition: A query that returns the rows in one table that have no match in another.

pandas-merge.label: pandas merge
pandas-merge.definition: Combining two DataFrames on matching key columns, like a SQL join.

deduplication.label: Duplicate records
deduplication.definition: Multiple rows that refer to the same real-world entity. What counts as a duplicate depends on the business definition.

bias-variance-tradeoff.label: Bias-variance tradeoff
bias-variance-tradeoff.definition: The tension between a model too simple to capture the pattern (bias) and one so flexible that it fits noise in the training data (variance).

evaluation-metric.label: Evaluation metric
evaluation-metric.definition: A number that summarizes how well a model performs, such as accuracy, precision, recall or AUC. Each one rewards different behavior.

accuracy.label: Accuracy
accuracy.definition: The share of predictions that are correct.

fraud-detection.label: Fraud detection
fraud-detection.definition: Identifying transactions or accounts that are deliberately deceptive. Fraud is rare, and fraudsters adapt.

missing-data.label: Missing data
missing-data.definition: Values that are absent from a dataset. Why they are missing affects how they should be handled.

outliers.label: Outliers
outliers.definition: Values far from the rest of the data. They can be errors or genuinely rare events.

experimentation-platform.label: Experimentation platform
experimentation-platform.definition: Shared infrastructure that assigns users to experiment variants, logs exposure and reports results, so teams can run A/B tests consistently.

batch-processing.label: Batch processing
batch-processing.definition: Computing over accumulated data on a schedule, such as nightly.

stream-processing.label: Stream processing
stream-processing.definition: Computing on events continuously as they arrive.

feature-pipeline.label: Feature pipeline
feature-pipeline.definition: The data flow that computes the inputs a model uses, both for training and for live predictions.

real-time.label: Real-time
real-time.definition: Responding within a tight latency bound, typically milliseconds to a few seconds, as each request arrives.

recommendation-system.label: Recommendation system
recommendation-system.definition: A system that suggests items a user is likely to want, using their history and the behavior of similar users.

ml-intake.label: ML intake process
ml-intake.definition: The way a company collects, evaluates, prioritizes and approves requests for machine learning work.

algorithmic-fairness.label: Algorithmic fairness
algorithmic-fairness.definition: Whether a model's decisions treat groups of people equitably. There are several competing definitions, and they cannot all be satisfied at once.

disparate-impact.label: Disparate impact
disparate-impact.definition: When a decision process affects one group at a materially different rate than another, even without using a protected attribute directly.

model-rollout.label: Model rollout
model-rollout.definition: Moving a new model into live use, from limited exposure up to full traffic.

unit-testing.label: Unit test
unit-testing.definition: An automated test of one small piece of code against an expected result.

training-serving-skew.label: Training-serving skew
training-serving-skew.definition: A mismatch between how features are computed or distributed during training and during live prediction.

reproducibility.label: Reproducibility
reproducibility.definition: Being able to rerun an analysis or model and obtain the same result.

model-serving.label: Model serving
model-serving.definition: Running a trained model so that other systems can request predictions from it.

latency.label: Latency
latency.definition: The time between a request and its response.

memory-footprint.label: Memory footprint
memory-footprint.definition: How much RAM a program needs while it runs.

rag.label: RAG
rag.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: look up relevant documents first, then give them to a language model to base its answer on.

llm-evaluation.label: LLM evaluation
llm-evaluation.definition: Measuring how good a language-model application's outputs are, often with rubrics, human labels or another model acting as judge.

prompt-engineering.label: Prompt engineering
prompt-engineering.definition: Shaping a language model's behavior by changing its instructions and examples, without changing the model itself.

fine-tuning.label: Fine-tuning
fine-tuning.definition: Further training a pre-trained model on your own examples so that its behavior or style changes.

hallucination.label: Hallucination
hallucination.definition: When a language model states something fluent and confident that is false or unsupported.

ai-agent.label: AI agent
ai-agent.definition: A language-model system that decides for itself which tools to call and which steps to take toward a goal.

tool-calling.label: Tool calling
tool-calling.definition: A model asking for external code to run, such as a search or database query, and then using the result.
